title: Tôi cảm thấy chóng mặt
summary: Different ways to say "I feel dizzy" in Vietnam, with the phrase to start with, reusable pieces, and related next steps.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Use this at a pharmacy, clinic, hotel desk, or with a guide when you feel light-headed or dizzy. Keep it direct so the other person knows this is a health issue, not small talk.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: Listen to each piece, then the whole phrase, so the rhythm feels connected instead of memorized word by word.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Tôi cảm thấy chóng mặt is the safer complete sentence. It says 'I feel dizzy' clearly and gives the helper a symptom they can act on.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.body: Health phrases need to be simple because the other person may need to act quickly or ask a follow-up. For "I feel dizzy", the useful move is keeping the useful noun or action in the center of the phrase. Use the related phrases below if the exchange moves one step further.

sections.title: Traveler insight
sections.body: In Health & Pharmacy, locals often answer with a short answer, gesture, or practical next step rather than a long explanation. That makes Tôi cảm thấy chóng mặt strongest when you say it once, pause, and let the other person show the next step. Show the document, symptom, location, or item connected to the need so helpers can act faster.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it before asking for medicine, a place to sit, a clinic, or help contacting someone.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Keep severe dizziness direct, especially with chest pain, fainting, or trouble breathing. Move to an emergency phrase when the situation needs urgent help.

sections.title: Local tip
sections.body: Point to yourself, sit if you need to, and show any medicine or condition note you carry.
